A team moves to .NET 9 and replaces

The belief: a time-ordered GUID like UUIDv7 is always insert-friendly as a clustered primary key.

That's what the standard promises. RFC 9562 says UUIDv7 is designed so that implementations that require sorting, database indexes included, can sort the values as opaque raw bytes, and that time-ordered values give better index locality because new values land near each other. PostgreSQL 18 ships a
function its docs call time-ordered. Even a quick check in C# agrees: sort

RFC 9562 defines UUIDv7 as a 48-bit big-endian Unix timestamp in milliseconds in the first six bytes, then the version, 12 random bits, the variant, and 62 more random bits filling bytes 8 to 15. In text, the first 12 hex digits are the timestamp: in the test,

SQL Server reads it from the other end
Microsoft's ADO.NET docs state that SQL Server compares

values with the last six bytes most significant, and their example sorts three GUIDs by their last group alone. The test showed the full order: the last group first, then the fourth, then the third, second and first, so the group where the timestamp starts is compared last. Microsoft documents this comparison for every version up to SQL Server 2025, whose list of new features doesn't change it; the runs here were on SQL Server 2022. So SQL Server orders a UUIDv7 by
first: random. Sorting those two test values, SQL Server returned the later one first, and the three lowest keys in its order had been generated 171,910th, 175,342nd and 51,983rd.
Each new key lands at a random spot in the clustered index, usually inside a page that's already full, so the engine splits it in two. That's the

cost the earlier article in this path measured for random-order indexes, and here it hits the table itself. Microsoft's index design guide lists the properties of a good clustered key, among them narrow and ever-increasing, and notes that a
, and isn't ever-increasing unless the values are generated sequentially. "Sequentially" means in SQL Server's order, not the RFC's.
Each key was inserted one row at a time, in the order it was generated: the .NET values were generated first, then replayed in that order.
